1	---
     2	name: repo-text-sweeps
     3	description: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
     4	---
     5	
     6	# Text & file manipulation
     7	
     8	Portable practices for searching, extracting, and rewriting text across a repository's files — grep/sed sweeps, renames and relocations, and the silent reference-breakage they leave behind. These are project-agnostic; they're the mechanics half of editing a codebase as text. (General software-engineering practices live in [the engineering-practices skill](../engineering-practices/SKILL.md); the merge-time relocation traps — git's rename detection, references that break with no conflict across a merge — live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md), "Merging across a file relocation".)
     9	
    10	- Deleting or renaming a file isn't done until you've grepped the repo for inbound references to it — a removed doc, module, or renamed path leaves dangling links, imports, or index entries behind that no test necessarily catches (e.g. a README docs-index link to a deleted file stays green). Grep the whole tree for the old path right after the removal and fix every hit in the same change.
    11	- When you relocate a file's *content or responsibility* into a new home — folding a doc into a pack, moving a function to another module, absorbing a routine into a skill — the original is now **redundant surface**, and reducing it to a tombstone stub (`# retired — see X`) is not finishing the job: the stub still costs a read, drifts from its replacement, and misleads anyone who lands on it. Delete the emptied original in the *same* change, and treat "did this move make anything else dead?" as a standing question after every restructure — the source you copied *from* is the first suspect. Don't wait to be told a leftover is redundant; a relocation that leaves two homes for one thing isn't done.
    12	- When renaming `foo/` → `bar/foo/`, a naive repo-wide string-replace of `foo/` → `bar/foo/` causes two silent corruptions: files already under the target namespace double-prefix (`bar/foo/file` → `bar/bar/foo/file`), and external URLs containing the string `foo/` get rewritten. Scope the replace to only internal path strings that need it, or do the replace then make a targeted post-pass reverting matches inside URLs and already-correct paths.
    13	- A grep/sed rename pass over a path (`foo/bar/baz.js`) won't match it when built from `path.join` segments (`path.join(__dirname, "foo", "bar", "baz.js")`) or wrapped across a line in a comment — those references survive the rewrite and break only at run time. After a mechanical path-rename pass, also search for the path's individual segment tokens and run the test suite; the test suite, not the grep, surfaces a missed reference.
    14	- An ordered specific→catch-all path rewrite can half-convert a reference the specific rule's trailing slash missed. Renaming `old/sub/` → `new/leaf/` with a slash-anchored rule (`s#old/sub/#new/leaf/#`) plus a catch-all for the parent (`s#old/#new/#`), a reference *without* the trailing slash (`path.join(root, "old/sub")`, a bare `git add old/sub`, a prose mention) escapes the specific rule, and the catch-all then rewrites only its **parent** — `old/sub` → `new/sub`, not `new/leaf` — a half-converted path that breaks at run time, not at the rewrite. Match both the slashed and bare forms, then grep the bare-dir form (at a quote / paren / line-end) and run the tests.
    15	- After `git mv`, re-read the file at its **new** path before rewriting it — an editing tool that tracks reads by path treats the moved path as never-seen and silently refuses the write, leaving the file stale (a failure that surfaces much later, far from its cause). When the move and the rewrite share a batch of tool calls, check each result individually; a single refused write is easy to miss in a batch.
    16	- A Markdown link carries its path **twice** — ``[`old/path.md`](old/path.md)`` holds it in both the bracket label and the parenthesized target — so a sed anchored on the `](href)` form updates the link target but leaves the visible `[display text]` reading the old path, and the doc points right while *reading* wrong. After an href-only sweep, also rewrite the display-text form (both plain `[old/path.md]` and backticked) and grep for the old string to catch the labels the href rule didn't touch.
    17	- To exclude a directory's own files from a reference search, filter by file **path**, not `grep -v` on line content: `grep -rn foo/bar | grep -v foo/bar/` (meant to drop the directory's own files) *also* drops every legitimate full-path reference elsewhere, silently undercounting. Exclude by pathspec instead — `git grep -n foo/bar -- . ':(exclude)foo/bar'` — which filters on which file is searched, not on what each matching line happens to contain.
    18	- To exclude vendored, synced, or generated files from a **structural** check that walks a tree (an orphan/reachability scan, a doc audit, a lint), derive the file set from git's tracked list (e.g. `git ls-files`) rather than a filesystem walk with a hardcoded path to skip — it can't desync when the artifact moves, and it stays correct when a new ignored directory appears. (Sibling of the pathspec-exclude rule above: that one separates a directory from its own files within a search; this one separates owned content from vendored/generated content.)
    19	- A zero-hit grep proves absence only at the case you searched. Code normalizes tokens away from prose case — an uppercase data table (`'KNEW'`), a SCREAMING_SNAKE constant, a lowercased slug — so a case-sensitive `grep knew` finds nothing and reads as "not in the codebase" while the entry sits right there, and a conclusion built on that phantom absence compounds. Before concluding a token is absent, re-run with `-i`; when history should have touched it, `git log -S<token>` is the cross-check that catches the miss.
    20	- When writing file content captured from a script or command output, use the `Write` tool directly — never `cp` from an internal Claude Code path (`/root/.claude/projects/...`). The tool-results paths are harness-internal and inaccessible to shell commands; referencing them via Bash triggers a permission prompt. Capture the output in context and pass it to `Write`.
    21

1	# Making changes to Claudinite without hurting consumers
     2	
     3	> **Status: provisional — beliefs, not law.** Every entry here says what we're *currently* doing
     4	> and *why we think* it helps. When an entry blocks a better change, challenge the entry rather
     5	> than contorting the change; being cited in this guide is not, by itself, a reason something
     6	> must stay. We'll solidify entries once they've earned it.
     7	
     8	Claudinite is vendored into every consuming repo, so a change here lands in many places, on the
     9	fleet's schedule, usually with no human watching. This guide collects what we currently believe
    10	about making such changes safely. It is a maintainer document for sessions working *in* this
    11	repo; it is not part of the vendored corpus.
    12	
    13	## First, know which channel the change travels
    14	
    15	Since the fleet moved to the tracked vendored mount (vendoring/DESIGN.md, phases 1–3 complete),
    16	the channel model is small — nothing reaches a consumer instantly, and nothing arrives outside
    17	its git history:
    18	
    19	- **The vendored corpus** (`engine/`, `packs/` — checks, prose, bundled skills) — each member
    20	  holds a tracked snapshot under `.claudinite/shared/`, converged **whole-set** to the canon
    21	  head by the nightly refresh and stamped with its provenance. Propagation lags one nightly,
    22	  lands as a reviewable commit on the member's `claudinite/maintenance` PR (auto-merged on
    23	  `auto-merge` delivery once the repo's checks pass, held for the owner on `review`), and the
    24	  rollback story is the same channel: fix the canon, the next nightly re-heals. A wrong
    25	  *blocking* check still fails every member's Stop hook — visible and recoverable, but
    26	  fleet-wide noise, so treat check changes as production changes.
    27	- **Migration notes** (`migrations/active_migrations/`) — the channel for anything convergence
    28	  can't express: renames of consumer-held wiring, declaration rewrites, one-off agentic steps.
    29	  Stamp-day-gated and idempotent; the note's `legacyPresent` telemetry says when the fleet has
    30	  moved and (for `retire: 'auto'`) retires the record itself.
    31	- **Copied artifacts** (pack `stubs/`, seeded configs) — these do **not** propagate at all. Each
    32	  consumer holds its own copy, which drifts silently unless a check enforces its shape. Changing
    33	  the source file alone only affects repos bootstrapped *after* the change.
    34	- **Bootstrap wiring** (the committed artifacts [bootstrap.md](bootstrap.md) seeds:
    35	  `settings.json` hook registrations, the two gitignore lines, the pack declaration) —
    36	  propagates through the nightly baselining's idempotent backfills on the same maintenance PR.
    37	  The discipline: a change here is written as steps that **converge from every layout in the
    38	  wild**, not just from the latest.
    39	
    40	Out-of-repo state remains the one channel git never reaches: a web environment's pasted Setup
    41	script is snapshotted at environment build. A change that moves what the pasted script calls
    42	needs the script's own probe to fail fast and a member issue asking for the one human action
    43	(re-paste).
    44	
    45	## Migrating a copied artifact (stubs and the like)
    46	
    47	Because copies won't move on their own, we currently migrate them through the conformance
    48	checks, in one Claudinite-only change:
    49	
    50	1. Change the source artifact in the pack (the stub under `packs/<pack>/stubs/`).
    51	2. Make sure the pack's conformance check enforces the properties that changed, with a `fix`
    52	   that says how to align (usually "re-copy the stub"). A consumer's own next session then
    53	   raises a blocking finding and performs the migration in that repo — no per-repo PR from
    54	   here.
    55	3. Keep the pack's `detect` fingerprint **tolerant of the legacy shape** while copies migrate
    56	   (e.g. a `LEGACY_*` list beside the current constant), so a fresh `--init` still recognizes a
    57	   not-yet-migrated repo and seeds the pack.
    58	
    59	Fleet-wide "everyone has migrated" telemetry exists — declare the rename as a
    60	[baseline migration](migrations/README.md), **in the same change that introduces the tolerance**: a
    61	tolerance that lands without its record has no signal that will ever retire it. Any legacy shape a
    62	tolerance keeps readable (an old path, a stub's old form, a legacy key *inside* a consumer's config
    63	file) is trackable the same way, `legacyPresent` reading whatever expresses the old shape. The
    64	fleet census probes every repo for the legacy shape and **auto-retires** the migration once none
    65	remain. While a migration's tolerance still lives inline (readers not yet consulting its
    66	`resolvePath`), keep it `retire:'manual'` and drop it deliberately.
    67	
    68	## Relocating wiring that consumers reference by path
    69	
    70	What we learned moving the sync hook between homes (#211/#213), and again retiring it (#385):
    71	the file is only half the change — every *reference* to its old path is itself a consumer-held
    72	copy that won't move on its own, and each needs a channel.
    73	
    74	- **Enumerate the reference holders before touching the file** — `settings.json` hook commands,
    75	  other canon scripts, the fleet routine's discovery probe, docs — then grep for the old path
    76	  afterward (the text-sweep skill owns the mechanics). Include state that lives
    77	  **outside the repo entirely**: a web environment's pasted Setup script is snapshotted at
    78	  environment build, where no check or baselining can ever reach it.
    79	- **Never break the channel the migration itself travels through.** Fleet discovery finds
    80	  members by the tracked `.claudinite-checks.json`; a probe that recognizes only a new shape
    81	  doesn't make noise like a wrong check — it **silently and permanently orphans** every
    82	  unmigrated repo, since discovery is what reaches them to migrate them. Same for the settings
    83	  registration: a session already running when the canon change lands still runs the old wiring,
    84	  so the old entry point must keep working until the member's refresh lands (that's what the
    85	  stable `engine/hooks/*-command` addresses are for — relocate what they call, not the
    86	  addresses).
    87	- **References nothing can reach get tolerance in the artifact instead** — prefer a probe that
    88	  *detects* staleness (and asks for the one human action) over hoping the stale copy keeps
    89	  working.
    90	
    91	## A vendored file executes in the consumer's context
    92	
    93	Canon files that ship into consumers — the whole vendor set (`engine/` and the declared packs) —
    94	run at their *landed* path inside the consumer's repo, not in the canon checkout they were
    95	written and tested in. Before changing one, audit every environment assumption against each
    96	context it ships to: **git discovers `.git` by walking upward**, so introspection from a vendored
    97	copy answers with the *consumer's* repo unless constrained to the expected toplevel (the
    98	`--show-toplevel` guard in `vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs` — an unconstrained `rev-parse HEAD` nearly
    99	stamped a consumer sha as canon provenance, #340); relative paths resolve against the vendored
   100	location; network access and credentials present where the file was written may be absent where it
   101	lands. The co-located header comment at the usage site carries each specific trap; this entry is
   102	the class.
   103	
   104	## Normalize requirements to canonical form at the door
   105	
   106	When a requirement arrives expressed in someone's local context — a schedule in a local
   107	timezone, a path from one repo's layout, a phrasing tied to one project's vocabulary — we
   108	currently translate it to its canonical form **once, on the way in**, and record only the
   109	result. A "nightly at 3:30 my time" request lands in the canon as a fixed UTC cron, stated in
   110	UTC and nothing else. The reasoning: the person who asked can carry the original framing;
   111	consumers shouldn't inherit it, and the canon shouldn't have to re-explain a conversion (or its
   112	edge cases, like DST) forever. If the origin matters for revisiting the decision, it belongs in
   113	the issue/PR that made the change, not in the shipped artifact.

1	---
     2	name: engineering-practices
     3	description: General software-engineering practices — naming by scope, single-source-of-truth with drift guards, GENERATED-file discipline, earning each dependency, verifying real platform behavior. Use before writing or editing code.
     4	---
     5	
     6	# Engineering practices
     7	
     8	General software-engineering practices, independent of any one project. (These are portable, shared rules; project-specific rules — architecture, test mechanics — live in the consuming repo's own docs. The portable git/GitHub-operational practices — branch/commit history, merging, automated-job branches — live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md); the mechanics of searching and rewriting text across files — grep/sed sweeps, renames, broken references — live in [the repo-text-sweeps skill](../repo-text-sweeps/SKILL.md); and the practices for writing trustworthy tests — see-it-fail, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, coverage gating — live in [the writing-tests skill](../writing-tests/SKILL.md); and how to investigate a bug and pin down its root cause — version-gap triage, re-deriving after a failed fix, probing for a real datapoint — lives in [the bug-investigation skill](../bug-investigation/SKILL.md).)
     9	
    10	- Name by scope/responsibility, not technology or mechanism.
    11	- Keep a single source of truth for derived or duplicated data — generate the rest from it instead of hand-editing, and have a test fail if it drifts. Split a fact across more than one place only when a technological constraint forbids a single home, and then have the drift-guard test state, in its own text, the two-or-more places it watches and why the split is forced — so an invisible coupling becomes a self-documenting, reviewed one, and the next reader knows the duplication is deliberate and where its other half lives. When the duplicate mirrors executable logic you can't generate from (e.g. a static list shadowing a set of predicate/matcher functions), drift-guard it by *executing the real logic* against the list in both directions — every entry accepted by some predicate, and every predicate satisfied by some entry — rather than parsing the logic out. When a value must be copied into files that can't share an import (a label spanning a YAML workflow guard and a JS module; a repo slug in prod code and its test), declare it as a `sharedConstants` entry in `.claudinite-checks.json` — its `value`, the expected per-file `counts`, and a `what` naming the places and why — and the basics pack's `shared-constants` check enforces the counts, failing when a rename leaves some copies behind. It counts the *flat* literal (comments included), so keep a guarded value on one line wherever it appears — an occurrence wrapped across a line break is invisible to the check and to a `grep`/`sed` rename alike. For a value that must stay in sync but *changes over time* (a version string bumped each release), set `regex: true` and give a pattern instead of a literal — the check then requires every match to be identical across the declared files, so the guard never needs re-pinning on a bump.
    12	- Honor separation of concerns in what you write — code comments and Markdown instructions alike: when file A uses or references file B (a module A imports, or a doc/procedure set A points to), A may state *what* it needs from B or *that* it delegates to B, but never restate *how* B does its job or re-spell the procedures B owns. B's mechanism lives in one place — with B. Copying it into A leaks B's internals across the boundary and springs the same drift trap as any duplicated source of truth: change B and A's paraphrase silently goes stale, with nothing to catch it. Point to B instead of paraphrasing it.
    13	- Name any file a test autogenerates with `GENERATED` in its filename (e.g. `foo.GENERATED.md`, `foo.baseline.GENERATED.json`) so it's unmistakable at a glance. Don't hand-edit a GENERATED file, and never resolve its merge conflict by hand: take either side to clear the markers, re-run the generator against the merged inputs, and commit its output. Hand-editing desyncs it from its source — and when the other branch changed the generator's logic, only a re-run produces correct values. Automate the "take either side" step itself where you can: assign the file a `merge=ours` `.gitattributes` entry (plus a one-time `git config merge.ours.driver true` per clone) so a conflicting merge on it resolves automatically instead of needing the markers cleared by hand first; `git config rerere.enabled true` similarly replays a manual conflict resolution automatically the next time the same conflict recurs.
    14	- Verify how a platform or runtime actually behaves against authoritative docs or a real run — not against a comment or a prior commit's claim.
    15	- Prove a *behaviour-preserving* optimisation actually preserves behaviour before trusting it — "it should be equivalent" is not evidence. Fingerprint the full outputs (hash them) and exercise the old and new paths across *every* branch (fuzz the inputs that select each), accepting the change only on a bit-identical match. And it is legitimate to leave a hot path un-optimised when the correctness risk of rewriting it outweighs the speed-up — record that as a deliberate call, not an oversight.
    16	- Earn each dependency: prefer a built-in (or a few lines) for a narrow job, and drop one when the assumption that justified it lapses.
    17	- Before adding production code for a raised edge case (a review's "what about scenario X?"), check whether the system's existing composed rules already produce the right answer — behaviour that emerges from a composition of independent rules (a pure reducer, a set of matchers) is often already covered, sometimes on more than one independent count. When it is, add no production code: pin it with a regression test — and an accept criterion under the relevant requirement, where you track those — asserting the contrast case too, so the test would bite if the rule interaction ever changed.
    18	- A bespoke how-to earns its place only by what it adds over authoritative external docs — our own failure modes, gotchas, and the exact path we ran. Before writing one, check it against those docs and keep only the additive parts; a guide that re-explains upstream (often less well) is worse than a link to upstream plus a short gotchas list. And document/recommend only a path you've actually run, not the "standard" or seemingly-better one you haven't.
    19	- Resilience that swallows errors destroys observability — during development, before a solution is proven right, add debugging information first, and remove it later.
    20	- When automating a task that requires live AI conversation context (e.g., a reflection pass over a session), hook it to an existing human workflow event rather than background infrastructure — shell hooks lack conversation access and fire at per-turn granularity, not session-end. The cheapest trigger is often a change to an existing command's definition.
    21	- In a pipeline or CI workflow, treat expected, handled outcomes (known-bad inputs, anticipated stops) as clean exits with a comment — not failures. Reserve the failure signal for genuine breakage; a red run should always be a surprise.
    22	- A live fetch that works on your machine can fail from CI or a sandbox (403/400, a CAPTCHA wall) because the *datacenter IP* is blocked, not the User-Agent — browser-like headers won't change that. Route the fetch through a residential-proxy service (these usually render JS too, so a single-page app records real content) rather than tweaking headers; treat targets that stay blocked even through a proxy as un-cacheable.
    23	- A cloud/root setup script may start in the repo's *parent* directory, not the checkout — a bare `npm ci` / build there finds no manifest and silently does nothing, surfacing much later as a confusing missing-deps error. Make the setup script `cd` into the checkout before running anything.
    24	- A `Cannot find module …` (or other missing-dependency) error on a *fresh* checkout almost always means the install hasn't run there yet, not a code bug — `node_modules` and other vendored dependency dirs start empty on a clone and on an ephemeral CI/sandbox checkout. Run the install and re-run before hunting for a code-level cause.
    25	- Collapse a property tracked in more than one place (a spec tag, a side manifest, a per-item field) into a single source of truth, preferring a *structural* classifier — one derived from where the item lives (its folder or path) — over a hand-set field: a structural classifier has no field to forget to update and can't desync from the item it classifies.
    26	- Avoid a default value; require it explicitly, or make it structural (derived from where the thing lives). A default moves the real value into a fallback (`x || DEFAULT`) plus a comment documenting it — two things that drift, neither visible at the call site — all to save a little typing. When automation maintains many instances of a config (a fleet of repos, generated project files), have the automation **materialize the explicit value into every file it maintains** instead of interpreting absence: the knob then sits visibly in the exact file where anyone would go to change it, and a missing key becomes drift the automation repairs rather than a case code must interpret (e.g. the fleet baselining writing `"maintenance": { "delivery": "auto" }` into each member's `.claudinite-checks.json`).
    27	- When a check that walks a file tree (an orphan/reachability scan, a doc audit, a lint) must ignore files you don't own — a synced submodule, a vendored dependency, generated output — derive its file set from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with a hardcoded path-to-skip. There's no exclude path to maintain, it can't desync when an artifact moves, and it stays correct when a new gitignored directory appears. Git already knows what you own; tracked vs. ignored is the exact distinction.
    28	- A check that scans source for a forbidden token (a banned API, an impure import, a DOM specific) must match *code, not prose* — strip comments before you match, or a comment that merely names the token (`// saved in chrome.storage`) fails the build over an English sentence, and the next author who documents the very rule you're enforcing trips it. Strip *string-aware*: a `//` inside `"https://…"` is not a comment, and blindly deleting to end-of-line corrupts real code (and can hide a genuine violation later on that line). The corpus's reusable helper is `stripComments` in [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs); a project whose scan can't import it (e.g. a test that runs where the mount is absent) should inline the same string-aware pass and point a comment back at that canonical source.
    29	- A comment should carry the *why* or a cross-file relationship the code can't state itself — not a fact already reconstructable from same-file code plus a known convention (a restated fact drifts out of sync as the code changes, silently). When a comment must name another file, state its exact path in exactly one canonical place and have every other mention point at that reference or the concept, not re-spell the path — a path repeated across many comments turns every future move into comment-churn the code itself never needed.

# `vendoring/` — how the corpus ships into consumers

Canon-internal machinery (never itself vendored, #385): compute a consumer's **vendor set**
from its pack declaration and converge the consumer's tracked `.claudinite/shared/` to it.
The decision record — why a tracked vendored mount, its phases, the anti-rewind guards —
is [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md); the adoption procedure that first runs this machinery is
[bootstrap.md](../bootstrap.md).

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| [`compute-vendor-set.mjs`](compute-vendor-set.mjs) | The **vendor-set computation**: a repo's pack declaration → the corpus file set that repo persists under `.claudinite/shared/` (the `engine/` root minus tests and root docs, plus the declared packs with their `requires` closure — each pack's bundled skills riding its own tree). Verified import-closed before it is returned. |
| [`apply-vendor-set.mjs`](apply-vendor-set.mjs) | The **vendor writer**: whole-set convergence of a target's `.claudinite/shared/` plus the provenance stamp (`claudinite.updated` / `claudinite.ref`), erroring **before any write** — with the #328 anti-rewind guards (a passed `--ref` must equal the canon checkout's HEAD; the target's prior stamped ref must be an ancestor). |

Both run **from the canon tree** (a checkout or a fetched snapshot) *against* a consumer
checkout — vendoring is done *on* a project, never *by* it. The regular updater is the
nightly baselining worker performing the equivalent writes over MCP; adoption and an
on-demand refresh run these directly.

The session-start orchestration the vendored files provide lives in
[`engine/hooks/`](../engine/hooks/) (the wired `*-command` entry points) and
[`engine/pack_loader/`](../engine/pack_loader/) — see those folders. The legacy
fetch-at-session-start mount (the tracked `sync-claudinite.sh` hook) retired with
phase 3 ([DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md)); every member runs from its committed snapshot.

Don't `curl` the run's status instead: in a sandboxed session `api.github.com` is proxy-blocked and returns an error body that never matches a success pattern, so a `curl`/`Monitor` poll silently reports "still running" until it times out.

1	# Flutter
     2	
     3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for Flutter / Dart codebases — true for any Flutter project
     4	read cold. Earned in missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers (a Firebase-backed, location-driven app with an
     5	executable-requirements UI suite); keep anything project-specific in the consuming repo's docs.
     6	
     7	## Architecture: ports out of the widget tree
     8	
     9	- **Widgets depend on ports, never on plugins.** Every platform/backend concern (location, auth,
    10	  push, backend calls, the clock) enters the UI as a hand-written abstract interface with pure-Dart
    11	  value types; plugin adapters (`geolocator`, `firebase_*`, `google_sign_in`, …) implement them and
    12	  are constructed **only** in `main.dart`. A plugin type leaking into a screen (a geolocator
    13	  `Position`, a `FirebaseFunctionsException`) is a defect: it silently couples every widget test to
    14	  the plugin's platform channels.
    15	- **Enforce the boundary with a committed import-scan test** (dart:io over `lib/ui/`, `lib/screens/`
    16	  looking for forbidden import prefixes). The analyzer won't stop a convenient leak; a five-line
    17	  test does.
    18	- **Ship the fakes in the package** (`lib/testing/`): scripted fakes for each port that also
    19	  *record* what the UI asked of them, plus a `FakeWorld` bundling them with a pinned clock and the
    20	  real app shell. Both the app's own tests and any sibling test package (e.g. an
    21	  executable-requirements suite) import one fake world — never two parallel ones.
    22	- **Extract the root shell into a widget** (`lib/app.dart`) taking the ports as parameters, used
    23	  identically by `main.dart` (adapters) and the test harness (fakes). Tests must never rebuild a
    24	  parallel MaterialApp — actuals come from the shipped shell.
    25	- **Inject the clock.** Any widget that formats or compares times takes a `Clock` port; relative
    26	  time rendered from `DateTime.now()` is untestable and drifts goldens.
    27	
    28	## Widget tests and goldens
    29	
    30	- **Load real fonts before any golden** — the test binding defaults to the glyph-less Ahem stub
    31	  (text renders as boxes). Parse `FontManifest.json` from the root bundle and `FontLoader` every
    32	  family (strip the `packages/<pkg>/` prefix so plain family names resolve), which also loads
    33	  MaterialIcons; bundle text faces (e.g. Roboto) in the test package's pubspec. Watch for styles
    34	  that don't inherit the theme's family — `ButtonStyle`/`styleFrom` text styles are the classic
    35	  leak; pin `fontFamily` there explicitly.
    36	- **Never `pumpAndSettle` around indeterminate progress indicators** — they schedule frames
    37	  forever and the call never returns. Use fixed-duration pumps (`pump()` then
    38	  `pump(Duration(...))`); this also makes an in-flight state (a spinner mid-send) a deterministic,
    39	  golden-capturable frame. Corollary: after `tap()`, pump **twice** — one frame applies state, the
    40	  fixed-duration pump advances implicit animations (ink ripples, color lerps) past the capture.
    41	- **Anything that fetches must be injectable**: map tile providers, avatar images. Widget tests
    42	  block real HTTP (a 400-returning stub client), so a `NetworkImage`/network `TileProvider` in the
    43	  tree means error boxes, not screenshots. Provide a deterministic in-memory substitute (a
    44	  canvas-drawn `ImageProvider` works and needs no asset files).
    45	- **Fix the viewport per suite**: set `tester.view.physicalSize` and `devicePixelRatio` to one
    46	  phone-shaped size (and reset in teardown) so layout — and therefore goldens — can't drift with
    47	  the harness default.
    48	- **Async lifecycle guards need an epoch counter.** A `start()` that awaits (permission check,
    49	  first fix) can re-arm streams/timers after `stop()`/dispose ran mid-await; bump an epoch in
    50	  `stop()` and bail after every await if it changed. The symptom (leaked GPS subscription after
    51	  sign-out) is invisible in tests that don't await realistically.
    52	
    53	## Toolchain habits
    54	
    55	- **Verify plugin APIs against the installed source, not memory.** Major Flutter plugins break
    56	  their APIs often (google_sign_in v7's `authenticate()`, flutter_map v7+'s options, geolocator's
    57	  settings objects); resolved versions live in the pub cache
    58	  (`~/.pub-cache/hosted/pub.dev/<pkg>-<ver>/lib/`) — read them before writing against them.
    59	- **`flutter analyze` at zero issues** (infos included) is the bar a suite holds; lints that fight
    60	  a deliberate convention (e.g. `file_names` vs. leaf-id case filenames) get disabled narrowly in
    61	  that package's `analysis_options.yaml` with the reason as a comment.
    62	- **Sandboxed/CI runners**: `flutter test` can stall for minutes at teardown on GPU-less containers
    63	  with dropped sockets. The pattern that holds: stream output, kill the process group the moment
    64	  the definitive marker prints (`All tests passed!` / `Some tests failed`), watchdog-kill on output
    65	  silence. On healthy machines plain `flutter test` is equivalent — keep the wrapper thin.
    66	- **The web sandbox ships no Flutter SDK.** Claude Code on the web boots without Flutter, so tests,
    67	  `flutter analyze`, and golden regen can't run until it's installed. Install belongs in the
    68	  environment **image** (built once, snapshotted, reused) — never a per-session hook that reinstalls
    69	  every start. This pack declares that need in its `env` block ([pack.mjs](pack.mjs)); a project pastes
    70	  one generic `environment-setup-command.sh` that runs every active pack's requirement via
    71	  [engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs](../../engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs) and asserts it at session start (see [bootstrap.md](../../bootstrap.md)
    72	  Part 9).

1	# AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model)
     2	
     3	Portable, project-agnostic gotchas for the AWS Serverless Application Model and the API-Gateway/CloudFront stack it deploys — true for any SAM project read cold.
     4	
     5	- **`BuildMethod: esbuild` strips the entry's subdirectory from the Handler path.** With a single entry point in a subdirectory (`EntryPoints: [src/handler.mjs]`), SAM's esbuild builder writes the bundle to `<artifact-root>/handler.js` — esbuild's default `outbase` is the entry's own dir, so the subdirectory is dropped. Set `Handler: handler.handler`, not `src/handler.handler`. `sam build` succeeds either way; the wrong value fails only at first invoke with `Runtime.ImportModuleError: Cannot find module 'src/handler'`.
     6	- **esbuild must be a regular `dependency`, not a `devDependency`.** SAM's esbuild builder runs a *production-only* `npm install` in its scratch dir, so a `devDependency` esbuild is skipped and the build fails with "Cannot find esbuild." Declare it in `dependencies` (it isn't bundled into the artifact unless the handler imports it), or put it on the runner's `PATH` before `sam build`.
     7	- **CloudFront won't forward `Authorization` via a *custom* origin-request policy** — a custom `AWS::CloudFront::OriginRequestPolicy` listing `Authorization` is rejected at deploy ("The parameter Headers contains Authorization that is not allowed"). To forward it to the origin while keeping it out of the cache key (so public GETs share one cached entry), attach the **managed** `AllViewerExceptHostHeader` policy (id `b689b0a8-53d0-40ab-baf2-68738e2966ac`) plus a custom cache policy that omits `Authorization`. Cache key and origin forwarding are independent controls — a `CachePolicy` defines the cache key, an `OriginRequestPolicy` defines what reaches the origin — so set them separately to cache public reads yet still deliver `Authorization` for authenticated writes. Use the *ExceptHostHeader* variant specifically: forwarding the viewer `Host` to an API Gateway origin returns 403.
     8	- **A deploy role must be able to drive the transform and CloudFront, or change-set creation fails with the real reason hidden.** The `Serverless-2016-10-31` transform runs as a macro, so the deploy principal needs `cloudformation:*`, and CloudFront management needs `cloudfront:*`, both at `Resource: "*"` (scope the *data-plane* grants to your stack instead). Under-scoping fails at change-set creation, and `sam deploy` surfaces only `Waiter ChangeSetCreateComplete failed` — the actual `AccessDenied` is visible only in the CloudFormation console's **Change sets** tab. Don't paper over it with `AdministratorAccess`.
     9	- **A brand-new AWS account can't create a CloudFront distribution until AWS verifies it.** The deploy fails `AccessDenied: Your account must be verified before you can add new CloudFront resources` — an account-level anti-abuse gate, not an IAM or template bug, so it is unfixable in code. Open a Support case to get the account verified, and launch against the origin URL directly meanwhile.
    10	- **A failed first `CREATE` must be cleaned up before you retry.** A stack left in `ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` (and a SAM managed-bucket stack stuck in `REVIEW_IN_PROGRESS`) can only be *deleted*, never updated — retrying an update errors. And any resource with `DeletionPolicy: Retain` survives the rollback orphaned, so the retry then fails `already exists` until you delete the orphan too.
    11	- **API Gateway HTTP API (v2) rejects a `chrome-extension://` origin in CORS `AllowOrigins`** with `BadRequestException: Invalid format for origin`, accepting only `http(s)://…` or `*`. An API fronted by a browser-extension (or other non-`http`) origin must therefore set `AllowOrigins: ['*']` and rely on its **JWT authorizer**, not CORS, as the security boundary.
    12	- **A CDN cache hit is served before the request reaches the origin or its authorizer**, so you cannot enforce request auth on a *cacheable* read without edge compute (Lambda@Edge) — and keying the cache per token destroys the hit rate that justified caching. Treat cacheable endpoints as public by design, and protect only uncached (write / per-user) paths at the authorizer.
    13	- **Prefer a short CloudFront TTL over per-write cache invalidation.** Invalidation is billed per path beyond a small monthly free allowance, so a write-through design that invalidates on every write is a cost trap; a short TTL plus optimistic local rendering hides the propagation delay from the writer at no per-request charge.
    14	- **Bundle the AWS SDK into the Lambda artifact rather than relying on the managed runtime's copy.** The runtime doesn't ship every SDK sub-package (a missing one fails only at invoke), and its bundled SDK minor version drifts under you over time. Declare and bundle the SDK packages you import, and pin a non-EOL runtime explicitly rather than letting it float.
    15	- **Review the change set before applying — `Replacement: True` on a stateful resource is a data-loss hard stop.** Replacement creates a *new, empty* resource and the old data does not follow; a DynamoDB table shows it whenever an immutable property (its `KeySchema`/`AttributeDefinitions`) changes. Enable stack **termination protection** too — it's a one-time CLI/API call (`update-termination-protection`), not expressible in the template body.
    16	- **Adding a DynamoDB GSI does not backfill existing items.** The `UpdateTable` is additive and indexes only items that already carry the index's key attributes, so rows written before the GSI stay invisible to it until each is rewritten with those attributes. Plan an explicit backfill pass if pre-existing data must appear in the new index.
    17	- **A custom request header turns even a public GET into a preflighted CORS request.** Any non-simple header (e.g. a client-version header) makes the browser send an `OPTIONS` preflight, so the API's CORS `AllowHeaders` must list that header or the real request is blocked *in the browser* — while server-side unit tests that never run the CORS layer stay green. Add each custom header to the allowed-headers list.
    18	- **Reach AWS from a session with the AWS CLI or a boto3 script — there is no AWS MCP tool.** A stack's real state comes from a CLI call (`aws cloudformation describe-stacks …`), which is the authoritative live status — the last green deploy workflow only reports the last *deploy*, not the current stack state. The CLI is **not pre-installed on the cloud/web runner** (nor `boto3`/`sam`), so declare its install in the **environment setup script** (`pip install awscli`, or the official bundle) rather than per session; point it at the sandbox proxy's CA bundle (`AWS_CA_BUNDLE`) if a call fails TLS verification.

Confirm such a run through the GitHub API/MCP tools: `get_job_logs(run_id, failed_only: true)` — "0 failed jobs" means green — or, for a release build, `get_release_by_tag`. Don't `curl` the run's status instead: in a sandboxed session `api.github.com` is proxy-blocked and returns an error body that never matches a success pattern, so a `curl`/`Monitor` poll silently reports "still running" until it times out.
packs/grow_with_claudinite/skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md:12:- **The routine's own in-session steps reach GitHub through the session's MCP tools — never a REST client or a `GITHUB_TOKEN`.** This is the corollary of the rule above: the steps a routine runs *itself* operate over the repos the session was granted, which the MCP GitHub tools already cover, so they need no token. A REST client, a raw `api.github.com` `fetch`, or a `process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN` read in in-session code (a migration pass, an agent-stage worker doc's steps) is the tell that the step was mis-built as if it were the CI *executor* — and it will 401 in the MCP-only session it's scheduled in, silently turning the run into a no-op. Only the part that genuinely needs the broader credential moves to a dispatch-only executor; everything else is MCP. *Diagnosing* whether in-session code can reach a host: probe with a tool that honors the sandbox's `HTTPS_PROXY` — `curl` does — never a bare `node -e "fetch(...)"`, whose global `fetch` ignores `HTTPS_PROXY` and goes **direct**, returning a verdict that bypasses (and so misreports) the proxy's real one.

content.content: packs/firebase/RULES.md:60:  same derived value (a geohash, a normalization), commit identical input→output vectors in both

- **Rate limits need a transaction.** A read-check-write cooldown is bypassable by firing calls
  concurrently; run the read + check + stamp inside `runTransaction` so concurrent invocations
  serialize. A thrown `HttpsError` inside the transaction aborts it and propagates unchanged.
- **Chunk batched writes well under the 500-op limit** and treat multi-batch fan-out as
  at-least-once: a mid-sequence crash plus client retry duplicates the early batches. Document
  the idempotency-key escape hatch even if v1 doesn't implement it.
- **Push is best-effort by construction**: notification failures must never fail the triggering
  call; clean up dead tokens on the *actual* error codes
  (`messaging/registration-token-not-registered` — verify codes against the installed
  firebase-admin, not memory or old blog posts).

## 3. Test logic pure, rules empirically

- **Extract decision logic into pure modules** (audience selection, filtering, formatting) so the
  default suite runs with zero emulators and zero mocks of the Firebase SDK.
- **When rules themselves are under test, test them empirically** with
  `@firebase/rules-unit-testing` against the real emulator — simulate each *exact client write
  shape* the app performs (create vs merge-update vs single-field token write) plus each
  forbidden shape. Reading rules and believing them is how the merge-semantics bugs above ship.
- **Cross-language contracts get mirrored test vectors.** When client and server must compute the
  same derived value (a geohash, a normalization), commit identical input→output vectors in both
  suites and diff the literals in CI — "both use the standard algorithm" is not a proof.

## 4. Deploy layout and aliases

- **Keep the Firebase project root self-contained** — the directory holding `firebase.json`, its
  `.firebaserc`, rules/indexes, and `functions/`. That root may be the repo root or a dedicated
  subfolder (e.g. `firebase/`); the CLI walks up to find `firebase.json` and resolves every path
  inside it *relative to that file*, so a subfolder needs no path edits — just run deploys from it
  (or pass `--config <dir>/firebase.json`). Keep compiled output (`functions/lib/`) and
  `.firebase/` gitignored.
- **Commit `.firebaserc` with named aliases and make the default the safe target** (see
  firebase-release for the full environment discipline). Deploy commands in docs always name
  what they deploy (`--only functions,firestore`) — an unqualified `firebase deploy` in a README

     4	
     5	## jsdom diverges from a real browser in ways a green test can hide
     6	
     7	A DOM faked with jsdom (the usual Node test-environment DOM) differs from Chrome in ways that let a passing test mask a broken production path — two that recur:
     8	
     9	- **`body.innerText` is null in jsdom.** Code reading `el.innerText || el.textContent` therefore falls through to `textContent` under test, which *includes* `<script>` / `<style>` text, `<select>` / `<option>` text, and CSS-hidden text that a real browser's `innerText` omits. A visible-text scrape can pass against cached HTML yet find nothing (or the wrong thing) in Chrome; treat body-text results as jsdom-optimistic and don't add a test that only passes because of it.
    10	- **`runScripts: "outside-only"` (the default) parses `<noscript>` into live DOM — the opposite of a real browser.** With scripting off, jsdom turns `<noscript>` content into real elements, so a `textContent` read looks clean under test but splices the `<noscript>` markup into the value in Chrome (which, scripting on, keeps `<noscript>` as raw text). Parse a script-free fragment with `runScripts: "dangerously"` to reproduce the browser.

     1	# Python
     2	
     3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for a Python package built around an optional
     4	heavy/native dependency (an ML model, a native audio/GPU library, a cloud SDK) that
     5	most of the codebase — and the whole test suite — must run without. The theme is one:
     6	**keep the importable core dependency-free, and gate every heavy thing behind an
     7	optional extra.** What stays here is the architecture judgment that has no
     8	false-positive-free static signature; the mechanical shape of the optional import
     9	itself (imported lazily, guarded with an install-hint re-raise) is carried by the
    10	`python-optional-deps` skill.
    11	
    12	## Keep the importable core dependency-free; heavy/native deps go in optional extras, not base `dependencies`
    13	
    14	The core of a package (its logic, storage, CLI, any web/dashboard layer) should import
    15	and run — and be **fully testable** — with only the Python standard library. Declare
    16	`dependencies = []` (or the genuinely-always-needed minimum) in `[project]`, and put every
    17	heavy, native, or ML dependency under a **named `[project.optional-dependencies]` extra**
    18	(`pkg[yamnet]`, `pkg[speaker]`, `pkg[dev]`), so installing the package is cheap and the
    19	heavy stack is pulled only when a user opts into the feature that needs it.
    20	
    21	The payoff is a test suite that runs anywhere with no ML/native toolchain: the offline
    22	and mock paths exercise the whole pipeline, and CI never has to install TensorFlow or
    23	Torch to be green. If a `pip install <pkg>` with no extra can't import the core, a heavy
    24	dependency has leaked into the base set — move it to an extra. Whether a given dependency
    25	is "heavy" enough to belong in an extra is a judgment about the package's shape, which is
    26	why this stays prose.
    27	
    28	## Provide a stdlib-only implementation behind the same interface so tests and offline modes need no extra
    29	
    30	Give the swappable interface a **dependency-free** implementation — a scripted/mock
    31	backend built on the standard library alone — alongside the heavy real one. That
    32	stdlib backend is what the test suite and any offline/`simulate` mode run on, so the
    33	full pipeline is exercised end-to-end without the ML or native stack ever being
    34	installed. The heavy backend is then just one more implementation of the interface,
    35	selected at runtime, never a hard import the core or the tests depend on. The clean
    36	shape is a tiny backend interface plus a `load_default()`/registry that lazy-imports the
    37	*selected* backend by name — so the module that wires backends together never imports
    38	any of them at load time, and adding a heavy backend never taxes the core.
    39	
    40	## Mark the availability-probe import as a deliberate unused-import suppression
    41	
    42	An import kept **only** to probe whether an optional stack is present (its name is never
    43	used directly — the code just branches on whether the import succeeded) is a real linter
    44	false-positive for unused-import (`F401`). Mark that line `# noqa: F401` and record the
    45	deliberate suppression, rather than deleting the probe or letting the warning ride.
    46	Whether an import is a genuine probe or an accidental unused import is a judgment a
    47	static scan can't make without a full unused-name analysis, so it stays prose.

1	# Research Project Working Procedures — a portable playbook
     2	
     3	This document defines **how the owner wants a research project run**, as a
     4	**bootstrap to drop into a new research project** from day one. It is written to
     5	be project-agnostic: it carries the durable working procedures and none of the
     6	subject matter, methods, or results of any particular study.
     7	
     8	It is aimed at the recurring class of research it is meant for: **run an
     9	algorithm over a set of similarly-formatted inputs, score it against
    10	user-provided ground truth, and improve the algorithm in repeatable, reviewable
    11	iterations.** Image analysis / computer vision is the archetypal case and the
    12	examples lean that way, but the workflow, ground-truth discipline,
    13	anti-overfitting stance, and session hygiene apply to research work broadly —
    14	read "algorithm", "input", and "render" as whatever they mean for your project.
    15	
    16	Treat it as a **default to adapt, not a contract**. When a new project needs a
    17	rule this one doesn't have, add it; when a rule here doesn't fit, say why and
    18	drop it. As you work a real project, replace the generic phrasing with that
    19	project's concrete specifics (its inputs, metrics, invariants) in *that
    20	project's own* docs — keep this bootstrap generic so it stays reusable. The one
    21	non-negotiable is the spirit: **show the work visually, prove each change against
    22	ground truth, never overfit the learning set, and leave the project resumable.**
    23	
    24	---
    25	
    26	## 1. The core loop — iterate on the algorithm, and *show* every step
    27	
    28	This is the cadence the owner wants, and it is the **deliverable style**, not
    29	optional polish. Follow it for every substantive algorithmic change.
    30	
    31	1. **Reproduce & diagnose — visually, first.** Start from the actual inputs.
    32	   Render the current behaviour and *look* at it before theorising. If a
    33	   decision hinges on a measurable fact (a colour/intensity split, a threshold,
    34	   an over-reach, a distribution), write a **throwaway diagnostic and measure
    35	   it** — do not guess. Cheap, disposable diagnostics beat argument.
    36	2. **Prototype in the scratchpad.** Build the change as a standalone script
    37	   first. Do **not** touch tracked code yet.
    38	3. **Show a comparison in the chat.** Surface a rendered **[ original | result ]**
    39	   side-by-side — and **[ … | ground truth ]** wherever scoring applies —
    40	   directly in the conversation (render it inline, don't just link a path). The
    41	   **picture leads**; numbers (accuracy metrics, the target quantity) come
    42	   *after* it as confirmation, **never instead of it**.
    43	4. **Get a read, then commit to the approach.** Only once the visual result is
    44	   right do you wire it into the tracked code. If a call is genuinely ambiguous
    45	   or is the owner's to make, ask **one** targeted question; otherwise proceed on
    46	   a sensible default and state what you chose.
    47	5. **Wire it in fully** — see *Definition of done* (§5).
    48	6. **Record it** as a numbered iteration note — what was wrong, what changed, the
    49	   metric delta, and **what you tried and rejected** (§5).
    50	
    51	### Show, don't just tell
    52	- Every algorithmic change is presented as a rendered comparison against the
    53	  original, and against ground truth when scoring is involved. Prefer a clean,
    54	  purpose-built **results figure** over a wall of metrics.
    55	- The presentation render is usually **not** the debug overlay. Favour a thin,
    56	  semi-transparent style that keeps the underlying data readable (thin lines,
    57	  mostly-transparent fills), and give a matched object the **same colour in the
    58	  result and the ground-truth panels** so over-/under-reach is obvious at a
    59	  glance. Tag objects with small ids that key into the metrics table.
    60	- Throwaway renders and diagnostics live in the scratchpad; only the **final
    61	  artifact and the code that regenerates it** get committed.
    62	
    63	### Interaction cadence
    64	Keep the owner in the loop with **pictures**, proactively. Ask a question only
    65	when a decision is genuinely theirs or the request is ambiguous — not to confirm
    66	work you can verify yourself. When you finish a unit of work, leave it committed
    67	and pushed so it can be reviewed or resumed from a fresh session.
    68	
    69	---
    70	
    71	## 2. Ground truth — user-provided, annotated, **never invented**
    72	
    73	- **The owner's annotations are the ground truth.** Every change is validated by
    74	  agreement against them, not against your own expectation of the answer.
    75	- **Ground truth is annotated, never fabricated.** Do not invent labels to make a
    76	  dataset scorable. If a dataset lacks the annotation a given harness needs, it
    77	  does not go into that harness (see §9 on validation tiers).
    78	- **Separate source-of-truth from generated artifacts.** The hand-annotation is
    79	  the source; the machine-usable ground-truth (registered masks, parsed labels,
    80	  normalized tables) is **generated from it and regenerated on demand** — never
    81	  hand-edited, because the generator overwrites it. To fix ground truth, **fix
    82	  the source annotation (or the extraction code) and regenerate**, then re-score.
    83	- **Make extraction deterministic and self-checking.** Same annotation → same
    84	  derived ground truth. Pin the things a human counted (number of objects,
    85	  number of regions) as assertions/tests so a silent extraction regression fails
    86	  loudly.
    87	- **Auto-detect annotation conventions from the data**, don't hard-code a
    88	  per-input flag. When the owner uses more than one annotation scheme over time,
    89	  detect which scheme an input uses from the ink/markup itself. Record the
    90	  **conventions** (what each colour / mark / region means) in a durable doc; they
    91	  are requirements, not incidental.
    92	- **Verify the annotation actually parses before trusting a score.** Inspect two
    93	  things: did the markup parse into the labels you expected, and did the derived
    94	  ground truth land correctly on the raw input (registration / alignment)? Keep
    95	  the review overlays.
    96	
    97	---
    98	
    99	## 3. Inputs — a small, similarly-formatted learning set
   100	
   101	- Projects like this begin with a **small learning set of similarly-formatted
   102	  inputs** (same modality, same acquisition regime, same annotation convention).
   103	  That is a feature — it lets you iterate fast and look closely — and a hazard:
   104	  it is small enough to overfit (§4).
   105	- **State the input format explicitly** (dimensions, modality, contrast
   106	  convention, expected content per input) so a mismatched new input is diagnosed
   107	  fast. Keep a one-line-per-input table.
   108	- **Name the primary target regime and what is out of scope.** A different
   109	  regime (inverted contrast, far denser or sparser content, a different scale)
   110	  is a *transfer* problem, not the main path — treat it as such until explicitly
   111	  in scope.
   112	- **Scale-awareness is a first-class concern.** An algorithm tuned for one
   113	  input scale (e.g. a zoomed view of a few objects) often fails on another
   114	  (a wide field of many). Know which regime you are tuned for, and measure the
   115	  gap on the other rather than pretending it's covered.
   116	
   117	---
   118	
   119	## 4. Do not overfit the learning set
   120	
   121	This is the discipline that keeps a small-set project honest. These are **hard
   122	constraints** — a change that violates one gets reverted even if it improves a
   123	metric.
   124	
   125	- **No single-input special-casing.** Every rule must generalise across the set.
   126	  If a fix only helps one input, say so and either generalise it or drop it.
   127	  Never key logic on a specific input's identity/filename.
   128	- **Keep decision rules free of the very prior you are trying to measure.** If
   129	  the project measures quantity *X*, no rule may bake in an assumed value of *X*
   130	  (that turns the measurement into an assumption). Prefer rules expressed in
   131	  terms the input **measures for itself** over fixed constants.
   132	- **Prefer scale-free rules over pixel/absolute constants.** Where a constant is
   133	  unavoidably tied to the current data's scale/resolution, **isolate and label
   134	  it** as scale-dependent so it is the first thing revisited on new-scale data.
   135	- **Name the hard constraint the task cannot trade away**, and tune to it first.
   136	  Some projects have a metric that is non-negotiable (e.g. a failure mode whose
   137	  cost dominates all others); identify yours, hold it at its required level
   138	  *first*, and optimise the softer metrics only underneath it. Make it explicit
   139	  so a later tuning pass doesn't quietly trade it away.
   140	- **Keep a registry of domain assumptions, each with a failure mode.** Choices
   141	  that encode a prior about the *subject or the instrument* (not pure
   142	  processing) are named, located in the code with an inline tag, and given an
   143	  explicit "how it fails on mismatched data" note. When a new input looks wrong,
   144	  the first diagnostic is *"which assumption did this input break?"* — and that is
   145	  only fast if the assumptions are written down. Flag the thinly-supported ones
   146	  (e.g. calibrated on a single example) honestly.
   147	- **Guard the wins with regression tests.** An input the owner has blessed as
   148	  "very good" must not silently regress when you tune for another. Pin its score.
   149	
   150	---
   151	
   152	## 5. Repeatable improvement iterations — the numbered notes, and *definition of done*
   153	
   154	Each accepted change is recorded as a **numbered iteration note** (pick a short
   155	tag and stick to it, e.g. `R1, R2, …`) in a running method-narrative doc. The
   156	point is that **the next session does not re-derive what this one already
   157	learned.**
   158	
   159	An iteration note captures:
   160	- **What was wrong** (the observed failure, ideally with the diagnostic that
   161	  showed it).
   162	- **What changed** (the rule/parameter and why, in scale-free terms where
   163	  possible).
   164	- **The metric delta** — before/after, per input, on the real scoring harness.
   165	- **What you tried and rejected, and why.** Rejected approaches are as valuable
   166	  as accepted ones; they stop the next session (or the next model) from walking
   167	  back into the same dead end.
   168	
   169	### Definition of done for an accepted change
   170	- **Source updated — never the generated artifacts.** (Regenerate them.)
   171	- **Artifacts regenerated** with the committed generators.
   172	- **Tests green**, and the **scoring deltas reported** (per input, per metric).
   173	- **Committed with a clear message and pushed**, so the work is reviewable and
   174	  resumable from a fresh session / another machine.
   175	- **Learnings cached**: the iteration note above, plus a pointer/update in the
   176	  session warm-up doc or the relevant reference doc **if the map or procedure
   177	  changed**.
   178	
   179	---
   180	
   181	## 6. Research phases, and spikes vs the main path
   182	
   183	- **Separate work into explicit phases**, each with a bounded deliverable, and
   184	  say which phase a piece of work belongs to. Defer the hard/advanced piece
   185	  explicitly rather than half-building it — e.g. get an intermediate output
   186	  trusted before building the final quantity that depends on it.
   187	- **Distinguish research spikes from the maintained pipeline.** Exploratory
   188	  scripts are worth keeping for reference, but the repo map must make clear what
   189	  "the pipeline" actually is versus what was an older spike, so a new session
   190	  doesn't mistake a dead branch for the main path.
   191	- **Keep a "known open items" / deferred list** so the boundary between "done",
   192	  "deferred by choice", and "not yet attempted" is never ambiguous.
   193	
   194	---
   195	
   196	## 7. Reading & summarizing source articles
   197	
   198	When a paper, tool, or reference method matters to the project:
   199	
   200	- **Write a self-contained notes file so the source never has to be re-read.**
   201	  Capture everything algorithmically relevant: the exact method/pipeline and its
   202	  parameters, the definitions and formulae, calibration details, and **sanity-check
   203	  values** you can validate your own outputs against.
   204	- **Explicitly record where your approach diverges from the reference and why.**
   205	  The divergence is often the whole point of the project; make it legible.
   206	- **State what you deliberately omitted** (material not relevant to the
   207	  algorithm — e.g. procedural/experimental setup detail, incidental statistics,
   208	  acknowledgements) and that you cross-checked against the full text — so a later
   209	  reader trusts the summary is complete for its purpose.
   210	- Note that upload paths for source PDFs are **session-specific and won't
   211	  persist**; the notes file is the durable artifact, not the upload.
   212	
   213	---
   214	
   215	## 8. Extracting images — samples vs illustrations
   216	
   217	- **Samples** are inputs you will run the algorithm on; **illustrations** are
   218	  figures that explain a method or a definition. Keep the two roles distinct and
   219	  store extracted figures alongside the notes that reference them.
   220	- **Render documents with a library, not an assumed system binary.** The
   221	  environment often lacks common tools (e.g. a PDF rasterizer such as poppler /
   222	  `pdftoppm`); use an in-process library instead. Locate embedded raster images
   223	  and render just the region you need, at a zoom high enough to read fine
   224	  annotation, with a little padding to catch ink drawn outside the frame.
   225	- **Verify identity when an extracted image should match an existing input**
   226	  (e.g. an annotated crop over an original) by an exact pixel diff — so you know
   227	  an annotation set is a labelling of the *same* data, not a new input.
   228	
   229	---
   230	
   231	## 9. Fetching more sample data from the outside
   232	
   233	- **Grow the corpus from public sources that match the input regime.** Curate and
   234	  **rank candidates by fit** = modality match × ground-truth availability × ease
   235	  of access, and record licence and provenance for each.
   236	- **Make ingestion a committed, repeatable fetch script**, not a manual download,
   237	  so anyone can reproduce the corpus.
   238	- **Respect the two validation tiers — and don't mix them:**
   239	  - **Full ground truth** (per-item annotations) → scores the *algorithm's
   240	    detailed output* (overlap / detection) on the real harness.
   241	  - **Aggregate label only** (a published summary number, no per-item
   242	    annotation) → validates the *summary quantity* the project reports, and
   243	    nothing finer.
   244	  Wiring an aggregate-only dataset into the detailed-overlap harness would force
   245	  you to **fabricate annotations**, which violates §2 ("ground truth is annotated,
   246	  never invented"). Keep a separate, mask-free validation path for those sets.
   247	- **External data is rarely drop-in.** Expect a scale/regime gap (§3) and
   248	  *measure* it with the appropriate tier rather than assuming the corpus is
   249	  covered.
   250	
   251	---
   252	
   253	## 10. Environment limitations — stay lightweight
   254	
   255	- **A fresh container has nothing installed.** Assume dependencies must be
   256	  installed each session, and keep the dependency set **small and lightweight** —
   257	  favour a compact set of core libraries over heavy frameworks (e.g. large ML
   258	  stacks) that are slow to install and awkward to run anywhere. Prefer a
   259	  lightweight solution that installs in seconds and runs anywhere.
   260	- **When a heavy or learned approach is genuinely the right tool, treat it as a
   261	  gated, isolated route** (documented, opt-in, scoped to the cases that need it)
   262	  rather than a new baseline dependency — and prove the lightweight route is
   263	  exhausted first.
   264	- **Route around missing system binaries with libraries** (see §8). Document the
   265	  exact install lines and any "install ad hoc, not in requirements" tools in the
   266	  warm-up doc.
   267	
   268	---
   269	
   270	## 11. Getting — and evaluating — algorithm ideas from the owner
   271	
   272	The owner will suggest algorithms and directions to try next. Treat these as
   273	first-class experiments:
   274	
   275	- **Take the suggestion seriously even when the project has declared a direction
   276	  "exhausted."** A suggestion may belong to a *different family* than everything
   277	  tried so far, which is exactly when it can break a wall the previous family
   278	  couldn't. "We already tried X" rarely covers a genuinely different approach.
   279	- **Evaluate it the same way as any change**: diagnose the wall it targets, build
   280	  the evidence that the wall is real (or isn't), prototype, and show a comparison.
   281	- **Beat the naive baseline, or drop it.** A more sophisticated or signal-driven
   282	  method is only worth adopting if it *measurably* out-scores the simple/uniform
   283	  baseline — sophistication is not accuracy when the guiding signal is noisy or
   284	  penetrates the structure unevenly, and a "smarter" local correction can lose to a
   285	  plain uniform one. Keep the roles of a signal distinct, too: a feature that is
   286	  excellent for *visualising or validating* a structure can be wrong for *defining*
   287	  it — gating the output directly on such a signal can erode the very structure you
   288	  are measuring. Always check the fancier route against the naive one before keeping
   289	  it.
   290	- **Document the outcome fully**, including the routes that hit a wall and *why*
   291	  (name the specific trade-off or signal that defeated them). If the idea needs
   292	  capabilities the environment won't allow (§10), record the concrete route to
   293	  try when that changes, so the thread is resumable rather than lost.
   294	- **Complementary routes are not competitors.** Two methods can attack the same
   295	  problem from different angles; keep both documented and say how they relate.
   296	
   297	---
   298	
   299	## 12. Record cross-domain applicability **out-of-band**
   300	
   301	When a sub-step of the algorithm plausibly applies to **another problem** beyond
   302	the current task, record it as a **short pointer in a dedicated side document** —
   303	a direction worth attention, not a validated claim, and it need not be certain to
   304	be worth noting. **Keep this speculation out of the algorithm itself**: code and
   305	inline comments stay strictly about the task at hand and its stated assumptions.
   306	This keeps the core legible and honest about what it is *for* while not losing
   307	genuinely useful observations that surface while building it. Add an entry
   308	whenever you build or substantially change a sub-step.
   309	
   310	---
   311	
   312	## 13. Continuity across sessions
   313	
   314	The owner works across many sessions and machines. Every session should end in a
   315	**resumable** state.
   316	
   317	- **Commit and push** finished units of work; leave the project runnable from a
   318	  clean checkout.
   319	- **Maintain a session warm-up doc** (the "read this first" map): what the project
   320	  is, how to run it, where the tuned parameters and the deep rationale live, and
   321	  the current numbers. It should let a new session skip re-reading the whole
   322	  codebase.
   323	- **Maintain a continuation guide**: where things stand, exact run commands, the
   324	  tuned parameters and *why they exist*, and the open items. Keep the headline
   325	  metrics current in it.
   326	- **When the owner asks for a different way to do something, capture the new way
   327	  durably — don't just do it this once.** A correction to *how* work is done (how
   328	  results are shown, what command to run, a naming/format convention, a step to
   329	  always take or skip) is a standing preference, not a one-off. Fold it into the
   330	  warm-up doc — or a reference doc linked from it — so the next session reaches
   331	  the same state without being told again. Prefer editing the doc that already
   332	  owns that topic over adding a stray note; if the change contradicts what's
   333	  written, replace it and say what changed. The test: *could a fresh session, with
   334	  only the warm-up doc, reproduce this new behaviour?* If not, it isn't captured
   335	  yet.
   336	- Follow the repo's **branch/commit/PR conventions**: develop on the named
   337	  branch, commit with clear messages, push; don't open a PR unless asked.
   338	
   339	---
   340	
   341	## 14. Reviving a prior session to **enhance this document** (not to continue the research)
   342	
   343	This document is meant to keep improving as the owner works. Some of the owner's
   344	process preferences live only in the **dialogue of earlier Claude Code (web)
   345	sessions**, not in any committed file. If the owner revives such a session and
   346	points it at this playbook, here is the instruction for that revived session:
   347	
   348	> **Your job in this revived session is to mine our conversation for *process and
   349	> working-style preferences*, and fold them into this playbook — NOT to continue
   350	> the research task itself.**
   351	> Re-read the whole dialogue and extract only the durable, project-agnostic
   352	> signal about *how the owner wants research run*: how they want results shown;
   353	> what they praised or rejected about the workflow (not just the algorithm);
   354	> ground-truth and annotation conventions; anti-overfitting rules they insisted
   355	> on; how they want articles summarized, images extracted, and external data
   356	> fetched; environment constraints they flagged; and how they hand off algorithm
   357	> ideas. For each item, strip out anything specific to this project's subject
   358	> matter and generalise it to the class of "run a CV/analysis algorithm over
   359	> similarly-formatted inputs, scored against user ground truth, improved in
   360	> reviewable iterations." Then propose additions/edits to the relevant numbered
   361	> section above (merge, don't duplicate; keep the principle-first phrasing). Show
   362	> the owner a diff of what you'd add and confirm the wording before committing.
   363	> **Do not run or modify the research pipeline.** If a preference contradicts what
   364	> is already written here, surface the conflict for the owner rather than silently
   365	> overwriting.
   366	
   367	To make revival productive, when the owner asks for it they should say **which
   368	session(s)** to revive (a link or a description) and, if possible, what topic the
   369	process discussion centred on — so the revived session knows where in the
   370	transcript to look.

packs/basics/skills/writing-tests/SKILL.md:14:- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. packs/basics/skills/writing-tests/SKILL.md:22:- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). packs/git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md:38:The default is to hold a PR until asked. Reverse that when a change's only reviewable output is produced by CI — an e2e/heavy-browser run, or a rendered artifact (a UI-snapshot pixel diff, a generated gallery) that can't be exercised in the local sandbox. Opening the PR is how the change is seen working and how failures surface, so doing it up front — rather than iterating locally first, which proves nothing for these classes — is the faster path to a working, reviewable result. Each CI iteration costs a full round-trip, so get the first one running as early as possible.

17. `pkill -f "<pattern>"` matches the invoking shell's OWN command line and kills the shell — silently dropping the rest of a chained command (exit 144). Remedy: bracket a character in the pattern, e.g. `pkill -f "[h]ttp.server 8099"`, and never chain it.
18. A stale `origin/main` remote-tracking ref makes work-scoped conformance checks report commits already on main as introduced by your work — `git fetch origin main` before believing or acting on a work-scoped finding.
19. Never `git checkout <old-branch> -- <paths>` to carry UNCOMMITTED edits onto a new branch — it restores committed content and destroys the uncommitted edits. Use `git checkout -b <new> origin/main`, or commit/stash first.
20. If a session's context has no pack prose / no owner preferences and no Stop-hook feedback between turns, the SessionStart hook did not fire — re-run the session-start hook command to recover, rather than proceeding without the rules.
21. Poll CI via the checks API (`get_check_runs`), never the legacy commit-status API (`get_status`), which returns pending/total_count 0 forever in a repo where nothing writes commit statuses.
22. Don't end a turn on a CI subscription/notification — if you won't sit and poll to green, arm auto-merge instead.
23. When a host is unreachable from the sandbox (egress-blocked), probe it with a throwaway path-filtered push-triggered GitHub Actions workflow on a hosted runner, read results from the job logs, and delete the probe + workflow before opening the PR.
24. In this sandbox, launch Playwright with NO `executablePath` (the browsers path env var is already set) and import from the ESM `index.mjs`, not the CJS `index.js` (a named import from the CJS entry yields undefined).
25. Keep ONE browser/driver script per session and re-point it via argv, rather than authoring a fresh throwaway script per check.
26. Known-noisy console output (favicon 404, ERR_CONNECTION_RESET) is not an application error — filter it out of smoke-test assertions rather than asserting a clean console.
27. Convert timezone/representation ONCE at the ingest boundary and keep a single internal representation; never let the other representation leak past that boundary.
28. Keep a CLI entry point's module-level imports dependency-free so subcommands that need no heavy/third-party dependency still run — import heavy deps inside the subcommand.

Also list the section headings of: `packs/git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md`, `packs/basics/skills/*/SKILL.md` (names only + headings of engineering-practices, writing-tests, unattended-agents), and `packs/node/RULES.md`, `packs/python/RULES.md`. And tell me: is there any pack for playwright / browser automation / visual verification anywhere in `packs/`?
